models.group: Classical governing equations and structural models
models.text: The suite should implement Newton's laws of motion, the equations of static equilibrium, conservation of linear and angular momentum, Cauchy's stress equilibrium equations, infinitesimal strain–displacement relationships, generalized Hooke's law, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, Timoshenko beam theory, Saint-Venant torsion theory, classical elasticity theory, Euler column buckling theory, beam-column interaction relationships, classical plate and shell theories, Castigliano's theorems, the principle of virtual work, complementary energy methods, stiffness matrix formulations and the direct stiffness method. It should also incorporate linear elastic analysis, geometric nonlinear analysis, material nonlinear analysis, elastoplastic constitutive models, von Mises and Tresca yield criteria, isotropic and kinematic hardening models, plastic-hinge models, large-displacement formulations, corotational beam formulations and nonlinear collapse analysis.

The classical and nonlinear environmental formulations should include Airy linear wave theory, Stokes higher-order wave theory, cnoidal wave theory, stream-function wave theory, Wheeler stretching, wave kinematics formulations, Morison's equation, drag and inertia force models, Keulegan–Carpenter relationships, Reynolds-number-dependent hydrodynamic coefficients, current profile models, logarithmic wind profiles, power-law wind profiles, spectral wave formulations, Pierson–Moskowitz spectra, JONSWAP spectra, directional wave spreading and combined wave-current loading models. Advanced alternatives should include potential-flow wave diffraction and radiation theory, boundary-element hydrodynamics, Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, Navier–Stokes computational fluid dynamics, volume-of-fluid free-surface modelling and coupled CFD–structural analysis where local flow complexity warrants them.

The suite should include Winkler elastic foundation theory, lateral pile resistance curves, axial shaft resistance curves, end-bearing resistance relationships, nonlinear pile–soil interaction models, elastic continuum soil models, Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, Drucker–Prager plasticity, Modified Cam-Clay models, cyclic soil degradation, distributed spring foundations, pile-group interaction models, nonlinear soil finite elements and coupled foundation–structure models.

models.group: Fatigue, seismic, ultimate strength and accidental response
models.text: The methods should include Palmgren–Miner cumulative fatigue damage, S–N fatigue relationships, stress concentration factor models, hot-spot stress methods, structural stress methods, rainflow cycle counting, spectral fatigue calculations, Dirlik's fatigue approximation, Paris–Erdogan crack growth, linear elastic fracture mechanics, fracture assessment diagrams, modal analysis, eigenvalue analysis, Rayleigh damping, Newmark-beta time integration, Hilber–Hughes–Taylor integration, response spectrum analysis, seismic time-history analysis, nonlinear pushover analysis, arc-length and Riks methods, reserve strength assessment, progressive collapse modelling, strain-rate-dependent plasticity and collision energy absorption models.

These should include beam–shell–solid finite-element coupling, global–local submodelling, nonlinear finite-element analysis, frequency-domain and time-domain dynamic analysis, stochastic environmental loading, response surface methods, Monte Carlo reliability simulations, first-order and second-order reliability methods, Bayesian updating using inspection information, digital-twin structural monitoring and physics-informed machine-learning surrogate models. Machine-learning and surrogate components should supplement rather than replace demonstrated structural mechanics and code-compliance calculations.

subtitle: In-place analysis, structural integrity, fatigue, buckling, earthquake response, foundations, installation and life extension.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the as-designed or as-inspected three-dimensional geometry of the jacket, including jacket legs, tubular braces, joints, pile connections, conductors, riser supports, boat landings and structural appurtenances. The structure shall initially be assigned its material properties, member thicknesses, corrosion allowances, connection characteristics and initial geometric imperfections where these affect nonlinear structural stability.

For a newly installed platform, the initial structural state may be taken as an undeformed or stress-free reference configuration before applying gravity, buoyancy, environmental loads and operational loads. For subsequent in-place or transient simulations, the initial state shall normally be the converged equilibrium condition under self-weight, permanent topside loading, buoyancy and other relevant sustained loads. The resulting member stresses, support reactions and displacements shall be retained.

For existing platforms, the initial conditions shall incorporate measured corrosion losses, member damage, initial deflections, cracks, residual stresses, foundation settlement and recorded structural modifications where relevant. Fatigue simulations shall begin with the appropriate accumulated fatigue damage or an undamaged reference state. Earthquake, collision, vibration and progressive collapse analyses shall begin from a defined pre-event equilibrium state, with initial velocities ordinarily set to zero unless the event occurs during an ongoing dynamic response.
bc: The foundation boundary conditions shall represent pile-head connectivity, pile penetration, soil resistance and the restraint provided by the surrounding seabed. Depending on the analysis, foundation conditions may be represented by fixed supports, elastic springs, nonlinear pile–soil interaction, distributed soil resistance or coupled geotechnical models.

The structural boundary conditions shall prescribe connection compatibility between jacket legs, braces, tubular joints, pile heads and topside supports. Connections may be modelled as rigid, pinned, partially restrained or nonlinear, according to the actual construction details.

Environmental boundary conditions shall apply wave, current and wind forces according to the specified water depth, wave kinematics, water levels, marine growth and loading directions. Seismic conditions shall prescribe the appropriate foundation acceleration or displacement histories. Operational boundary conditions shall apply gravity, equipment loads, deck reactions, drilling loads and crane loads at their actual structural interfaces.

For installation and transportation, temporary support locations, lifting-point constraints, barge supports, seafastening restraints and prescribed lifting motions shall be specified. Impact analysis shall define the contact region, impact velocity and interaction between colliding bodies. Progressive collapse analysis shall permit the removal or degradation of selected members, together with redistribution of load through the remaining structure.

calibration: Calibration should use measured structural responses from offshore jacket platforms, laboratory tubular-joint tests, instrumented load tests, structural health-monitoring records and documented offshore inspection programmes. Structural stiffness, connection rotational stiffness, joint flexibility, support restraint assumptions and damping parameters should be adjusted where justified by measured natural frequencies, mode shapes, accelerations, strains and operational deflections.

Hydrodynamic drag and inertia coefficients should be calibrated against wave-flume experiments, wave-current basin measurements and field data obtained from instrumented offshore structural members. Marine growth characteristics and surface roughness effects should be calibrated using inspection measurements and locally observed hydrodynamic response.

Pile–soil interaction parameters should be calibrated using site-specific geotechnical investigations, cone penetration testing, laboratory soil testing, instrumented pile load tests and, where available, field-measured foundation displacements. Soil stiffness, cyclic degradation and lateral resistance should be adjusted within ranges supported by the soil measurements.

Tubular joint strength and fatigue models should be calibrated using representative joint specimens, weld fatigue tests, hot-spot strain measurements and documented fatigue datasets. Nonlinear plasticity, local buckling, ultimate strength and reserve strength parameters should be informed by representative large-scale structural experiments and measured failure behaviour.

For ageing platforms, calibration should incorporate measured corrosion, wall-thickness reduction, crack dimensions, connection deterioration and observed structural changes. Data used for calibration should be distinguishable from independent data reserved for validation.
verification: Verification should include member-level analytical benchmarks for axial loading, bending, torsion, shear, beam-column behaviour and structural deflection. Three-dimensional frame and finite-element formulations should reproduce established linear-elastic responses and known stiffness and equilibrium properties.

Mesh convergence should be demonstrated for global jacket models and detailed tubular-joint finite-element models, with particular attention to weld intersections, stress concentration regions, contact interfaces and local buckling locations. Element formulations should be checked for shear locking, artificial stiffness, spurious modes and sensitivity to element quality.

Nonlinear structural analysis should be verified through load-increment refinement, convergence tolerance studies, equilibrium residual checks and benchmark problems involving plasticity, geometric nonlinearity, buckling, post-buckling and progressive member failure.

Dynamic response verification should include natural-frequency benchmarks, mode-shape comparisons, free-vibration tests, forced-vibration tests, damping implementation checks and time-step convergence studies.

Hydrodynamic loading should be verified using independently calculated wave kinematics, appropriate wave-force benchmarks and controlled comparisons for different wave and current directions. Seismic response should be tested using prescribed ground-motion records and independent response-history benchmarks.

Foundation coupling should be verified through pile load-transfer benchmarks, lateral pile response problems, support stiffness checks and force compatibility between the jacket and foundation models.

Pushover, reserve strength, accidental impact, progressive collapse, load-out, transportation, lifting and installation calculations should each undergo dedicated benchmark tests. Global equilibrium, transferred reactions, energy balance where applicable, load-path continuity and structural stability should be checked at every relevant stage.
validation: Validation should compare predicted platform natural frequencies, damping, mode shapes, member strains and displacements against independent offshore monitoring measurements.

Wave and current loading predictions should be assessed using instrumented offshore platforms or physical-model experiments for which environmental conditions, structural geometry and measured response are sufficiently documented.

Tubular-joint fatigue and ultimate strength predictions should be compared against independent experimental joint tests covering representative geometries, thickness ratios, load combinations and failure modes.

Pile foundation predictions should be validated using full-scale pile load tests and observed axial and lateral foundation behaviour. Where field data are unavailable, appropriate physical-model tests can support validation within their scale and soil-condition limitations.
Structural collapse and reserve strength predictions should be tested against large-scale jacket experiments, published experimental benchmarks and documented damaged-structure response cases.

Installation analyses should be validated against recorded crane tensions, lifting reactions, launching trajectories, upending angles and transportation response where such industrial measurements are available.
Life-extension predictions should be assessed against subsequent inspection observations, measured deterioration and independent structural reassessments.

Validation reports should document measurement uncertainty, modelling assumptions, discrepancies, critical response quantities and the conditions within which predictions have demonstrated acceptable accuracy.

geometry.text: Fixed steel jackets, lattice platforms, tubular legs, horizontal and diagonal braces, pile foundations, conductor guides, boat landings, deck supports, tubular joints and integrated platform structures.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: The suite should accept STEP (.step, .stp), including appropriate AP203, AP214 and AP242 representations; IGES (.iges, .igs); Parasolid (.x_t, .x_b); ACIS SAT/SAB (.sat, .sab); AutoCAD DXF (.dxf); DWG (.dwg) through a compatible licensed or supported reader; IFC (.ifc); and CAD surface representations using NURBS geometry. These formats should support imported tubular members, structural assemblies, deck frames, welded connections, stiffeners, pipe supports and pile geometries.

The suite should support SDNF (.sdnf), CIS/2 steelwork exchange representations, IFC-based structural models, structural node-and-member models in validated XML, JSON or CSV schemas, and solver-specific structural input formats through dedicated import adapters. Structural geometries should retain member connectivity, section orientation, joint offsets, cross-sectional dimensions, member eccentricities and global coordinate references.

The suite should accept Nastran bulk-data files (.bdf, .nas), Abaqus input files (.inp), ANSYS-compatible mesh files (.cdb), Gmsh (.msh), MED (.med), UNV (.unv), VTK (.vtk, .vtu) and Exodus (.e, .exo) where appropriate readers and element-type mappings are implemented. These representations are useful for member-level, tubular joint, shell, solid, nonlinear and local stress analyses.

The suite should also accommodate STL (.stl), OBJ (.obj), PLY (.ply), 3MF (.3mf), glTF/GLB (.gltf, .glb), laser-scan point clouds in LAS/LAZ (.las, .laz), E57 (.e57), XYZ point lists and registered photogrammetric meshes. Such inputs can support as-built jacket reconstruction, damage assessment and geometry verification, but may require surface fitting, structural member recognition and dimensional reconciliation before simulation.
